title: How Active Directory Replication Works and Where It Breaks
summary: Practical working knowledge of AD multi-master replication, the tools used to check its health, and the failure categories operators actually hit.
objective: Run a daily replication health check and correctly bucket a failure into a known root-cause category before escalating.
body_outline: AD DS is multi-master: any writable DC can accept an update; replication propagates it via the Knowledge Consistency Checker (KCC)-built topology.
Run repadmin /showrepl per-DC or repadmin /replsummary forest-wide; read the Inbound Neighbors section and the Last Failure Time column.

Root causes cluster into six buckets, checked in order: network connectivity, DNS name resolution, replication topology, authentication/authorization, directory database health, replication engine/scheduling.

Recognize events by number: 1311 (topology mismatch), 1925 (link establishment failed), 1388/1988/2042 (lingering object / tombstone lifetime exceeded), 2087/2088 (DNS resolution of replication partner).
quick_check: A DC shows 'No inbound neighbors' in repadmin /showrepl. What do you check first, and why?

title: The Five FSMO Roles and When You Actually Touch Them
summary: What each of the five Flexible Single Master Operations roles does, which are forest-wide vs domain-wide, and the transfer-vs-seize decision.
objective: Name each FSMO role's scope, state its function, and decide transfer vs seize for a given failure scenario.
body_outline: Two forest-wide roles: Schema Master (only DC that accepts schema changes), Domain Naming Master (only DC that can add/remove domains or application partitions).

Three domain-wide roles: PDC Emulator (password/lockout authority, default GPO target, forest-root PDC is the forest's authoritative time source), RID Master (allocates RID pools so SIDs stay unique), Infrastructure Master (fixes cross-domain object references; irrelevant once AD Recycle Bin is enabled forest-wide).
Rule: transfer whenever the current holder is online; seize only when it is permanently unavailable, because a seized role holder must never come back online still holding that role.
Placement guidance: minimize the number of DCs holding roles, keep them well-connected, keep the PDC Emulator reachable at all times.
quick_check: Which two FSMO roles are forest-wide rather than per-domain?

title: What Forest Recovery Actually Involves
summary: The shape of an AD forest recovery: when it's warranted, the high-level phases, and what you commit to losing.
objective: Explain when forest recovery is the right call, name the five recovery phases, and state what data is unavoidably lost.
body_outline: Forest recovery is a last resort for forest-wide failure (all DCs corrupted, compromised, or unable to replicate/accept changes) - not the answer to a single failed DC.
Five phases: identify the problem, determine how to recover, perform initial recovery (one clean DC per domain, root domain first), redeploy remaining DCs, cleanup.
You lose everything since the last trusted backup: new objects, updates to existing objects, and any schema/configuration partition changes - so backup currency directly bounds your recovery point.

Microsoft's forest recovery guide as retrieved explicitly covers DCs on Windows Server 2012 through 2022; treat Windows Server 2025-specific nuances as VERSION_CURRENT_WITH_CONTEXT until confirmed against that version's own documentation.
Practice this at least annually and after any Enterprise Admins/Domain Admins membership change - an untested plan is not a plan.
quick_check: Why must the very first recovered DC in the forest root domain get an authoritative SYSVOL restore, while subsequently recovered DCs must not?

title: Kerberos Authentication: The Checklist Before You Trace Packets
summary: The ordered, mostly non-invasive checklist Microsoft recommends before reaching for Network Monitor on a Kerberos failure.
objective: Work a Kerberos failure through the standard checklist (logs, infrastructure, ports, DC availability, DNS, time sync) before escalating to packet capture.
body_outline: Check Security/System event logs on client, target server, and DC for Kerberos/KDC/LSA/Netlogon-sourced events first.
Confirm client and target service are on separate computers where required, both domain-joined to trusted domains, and the target server's dependent services are actually running.
Verify required ports are open end to end: DNS 53, Kerberos 88 and 464, LDAP 389/636, SMB 445, RPC endpoint mapper 135, W32Time 123.

Use nltest /dsgetdc:<domain> /force /kdc to confirm a DC is reachable, nslookup to confirm name resolution, and w32tm /resync to rule out clock skew (Kerberos tickets fail outside the default 5-minute skew tolerance).

Only after that checklist is exhausted do you collect simultaneous Network Monitor traces on client and server and read for KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED, KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW, KDC_ERR_ETYPE_NOTSUPP, or KDC_ERR_S_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN.
quick_check: A user gets KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW. What's the fix, and which command checks for it directly?

title: Group Managed Service Accounts: What They Fix and Their Limits
summary: Why gMSAs exist, what they automate, and the one common platform (failover clustering) where they don't directly apply.
objective: Explain what problem gMSA solves versus a standard service account, and correctly identify when sMSA or a standard account is required instead.
body_outline: A gMSA is a domain account whose 240-byte password the Windows OS (via the Microsoft Key Distribution Service) manages and rotates automatically, by default every 30 days - no admin-managed password rotation.

It extends the older standalone MSA (sMSA, single-server-only) across multiple servers, so a load-balanced service farm can share one identity for mutual authentication without every instance needing the same manually-synced password.
Requires domain functional level Windows Server 2012+; gMSAs are not applicable to domains below that level.

Failover clustering does not support gMSA directly - services running on top of the Cluster service (a Windows service, an app pool, a scheduled task) can still use one if they natively support gMSA/sMSA.
Security note: a gMSA in a privileged group is exactly as risky as a privileged user account - audit group membership and resource access the same way.
quick_check: Why can't you put a gMSA directly on the Cluster service itself?
